say: A [genome-wide](/ʤˈinOm wˈId/) CRISPR screen puts a question to every gene: is this gene a hit? || There are twenty thousand candidate genes.
caption: ~20,000 candidate genes

say: But what is a CRISPR screen? || A screen tests which genes control a specific cellular behaviour or trait.
caption: what a screen measures

say: You set up an experiment. | Say, neuroblastoma cells, | and whether they resist iron-mediated cell death. || Then you switch one gene off, or on, | and see whether the outcome changed.
caption: perturb one gene, re-run the assay

say: Do that across the whole genome, | and you learn which genes control the behaviour you care about.
caption: repeat across the genome

say: A few of those genes are hits. | A hit is a gene where switching it off, or on, actually produces the effect you are looking for. || In a typical screen, only one in a hundred are hits.
caption: a hit: perturbing it produces the phenotype

say: You do not know which ones they are. || That is the whole point of running the screen.
caption: ~1% are hits  ·  you cannot see which

say: But testing all of them is often out of reach. | The readout is too slow, or too expensive. || So you get a budget: | one thousand genes, | five percent of the library.
caption: budget: 1,000 genes  ·  5%

say: Which thousand should you pick?
caption: which 1,000?

say: You don't have to choose all at once. || Spend the budget in rounds. | One hundred genes, ten times.
caption: 10 rounds  ×  100 genes

say: After each round you learn which of those hundred were hits, | and that answer can change what you pick next. || That is the loop.
caption: propose  →  observe  →  adapt

say: This is AssayBench-Loop: | one thousand three hundred and eighty-nine real CRISPR screens, split by time. || Train on the past, | test on twenty screens from the future.
caption: 1,349 train   ·   20 test

say: We can picture any strategy with a recovery curve: || the fraction of all hits you have found, | against the fraction of the library you have sampled.
caption: recovery curve

say: Pick genes at random, and you find hits at exactly the rate you sample them. || A straight line. | That is the thing to beat.
caption: random expectation

say: One way to fill that first round is to ask a language model. || It has read the literature, | so it already has an opinion about which genes are plausible, | before you measure anything.
caption: knowledge from papers, not from this assay

say: And it works. || Gemini three point one Pro finds hits at nearly five times the random rate.
caption: Gemini 3.1 Pro   ·   EF 4.71

say: But watch what happens as results come back. || The curve flattens. || The prior is strong. | The learning from feedback is weak.
caption: strong prior, weak adaptation

say: AssayFormer is the opposite animal. || A transformer trained across all thirteen hundred historical screens. || It takes the history as input: | every gene tested so far, and whether it was a hit.
caption: history-conditioned policy

say: It starts colder. || Before the first batch, it knows little about this particular screen.
caption: AssayFormer   ·   EF 4.83

say: But every round of feedback sharpens it, | and it keeps climbing.
caption: weak prior, strong adaptation

say: LLMs have a strong prior but weak adaptation. || AssayFormer has a weak prior but strong adaptation. || So use each one where it is best.
Let the language model drive the first three rounds. || Then hand the accumulated history to AssayFormer, | and let it run.
caption: handoff at k = 3

say: That is AssayLoop.
caption: AssayLoop

say: Five point seven times better than random. || Twenty-seven point seven percent of hits in the screen are found by sampling only five percent of the library.
And because the policy is learned from past experiments, | it improves as those accumulate, || with no sign yet of saturating.
caption: more screens  →  better policy

say: Biology in the loop. || Try it on our website today!
